Allene Synthesis: A Concerted Asynchronous Mechanism
Xinya Yuan, Jiashen Yang, and Shaozhong Wang*

ABSTRACT: The carbonyl−yne reaction, involving propargylic C−H
bond cleavage for carbon−carbon bond formation, is significantly less
developed than the classical Alder−ene reaction due to the linear
geometry and relatively weak nucleophilicity of alkynes compared to
alkenes. Herein, we report a Sc(OTf)
3
-catalyzed carbonyl−yne reaction
enabling the diastereoselective synthesis of multisubstituted allenes
from α-ketoamide-tethered alkynes with 100% atom economy and
excellent diastereoselectivity (up to 20/1 dr). DFT calculations support a concerted, asynchronous mechanism involving C−C bond
formation and propargylic C−H cleavage. Theoretical analysis suggests that the observed stereoselectivity arises from an interplay of
electronic and entropic effects in the transition states.
A
llenyl moieties constitute privileged axially chiral scaffolds
with broad utility across organic synthesis, pharmaceut-
icals, and materials science.
1−4
Their orthogonal π-systems
enable unique reactivity profiles, facilitating diverse trans-
formations including cycloadditions, cycloisomerizations,
allylic substitutions, and transition-metal-catalyzed cou-
plings
5−10
While classical allene syntheses typically require
stoichiometric reagents or multistep sequences,
11−14
catalytic
carbonyl−yne reactions offer an atom-economical, convergent
alternative for direct construction from alkynes and carbonyl
partners. Mechanistically, this transformation parallels the
classical ene reaction
15,16
but substitutes the “ene” component
with a propargylic fragment (Scheme 1a,b). Where classical
ene reactions engage an allylic C−H bond, an alkene C�C
bond, and an enophile, the carbonyl−yne variant utilizes a
propargylic C−H bond, an alkyne C�C bond, and an
ynophile (carbonyl group). Investigation of this “propargyl−
ene-type” reaction would provide a rational mechanistic
explanation and deeper understanding for the stereoselective
formation of multisubstituted allene products. Nevertheless,
achieving high diastereo- and even enantioselectivity for
multisubstituted allenes, particularly sterically congested
architectures, remains challenging.
17−20
Existing carbonyl−yne reactions
21
can present certain
limitations, such as a somewhat narrow substrate scope,
modest levels of stereocontrol, and mechanistic aspects that are
still being uncovered. Lewis acid catalysis might potentially
overcome these limitations by coordinatively activating
carbonyl groups toward alkyne nucleophiles.
22
Rare-earth
metal triflates exhibit exceptional oxophilicity, functional
group tolerance, and moisture compatibility, positioning
them as ideal catalysts for the carbonyl−yne transformation.
23
Herein, we report the first Sc(OTf)
3
-catalyzed carbonyl−yne
reaction for diastereoselective synthesis of multisubstituted
allenes from α-ketoamide-tethered alkynes (Scheme 1c). This
method features perfect atom economy, broad substrate scope
and exceptional diastereoselectivity. Mechanistic studies

effects in the transition states might control the stereo-

versatility of the resulting allenes through diverse downstream
transformations, including cycloisomerization and semipinacol
rearrangements for accessing complex dihydrofurans.

formation of 2a in 45% yield (Table 1, entry 10). The relative
stereochemistry was assigned based on X-ray of single crystal
diffraction study of its analog 2u (see SI for details). Using
Sc(OTf)
3

DCM, toluene, or PhCF
3

In contrast, the yield decreased significantly in dioxane (Table
1, entry14). Elevating the reaction temperature to 80 °C in 1,2-
DCE improved the yield while maintaining comparable
diastereoselectivity (Table 1, entries 15−16). Control experi-
ments showed that reduced Sc(OTf)
3
loadings led to lower
yields, and the carbonyl−yne reaction failed to occur either in
the absence of Sc(OTf)
3
or in the presence of Brϕnsted acid
HOTf, which could originate from the partial decomposition
of Sc(OTf)
3
(Table 1, entries 17−19).
With optimized conditions established, we next explored the
scope of the Sc(OTf)
3
-catalyzed carbonyl−yne reaction by
varying substituents on the ketone, alkyne, benzene ring, and
nitrogen atom. Similar to substrate 1a, alkynes 1b−1f bearing
aliphatic α-ketoamide groups with primary, secondary, or
tertiary alkyl substituents (Me, Et, phenylethyl, Cy, t-Bu)
underwent smooth conversion to allenes 2b−2f in 33−88%
yield with 5/1 to 8/1 dr (Table 2, entries 1−6). Alkynes 1g−
1k with arylated α-ketoamides reacted similarly, affording
allenes 2g−2k in 42−73% yield with 2.6/1 to 5.8/1 dr (Table
2, entries 7−11). Alkynes 1l−1u with primary, secondary,
tertiary alkyl, or phenyl substituents at the propargylic position
(Et, phenethyl, i-Bu, cyanoethyl, BnOCH
2
, 1-chloropropyl, 2-
(1H-indol-1-yl)ethyl, i-Pr, cyclohexyl, Ph) all produced allenes
2l−2u in excellent yields (up to 90%) with dr values up to 20/
1 (Table 2, entries 12−21). Substrates 1v−1z with substituents
(Br, F, NO
2
, Me, Ph) on the aniline ring linking the α-
ketoamide and alkyne units also performed well, delivering
allenes 2v−2z in comparable efficiency (Table 2, entries 22−
26). Finally, alkynes 1aa−1ab featuring benzyl or propargyl
groups on the nitrogen atom participated effectively, yielding
allenes 2aa (84% yield, 8/1 dr) and 2ab (67% yield, 5.6/1 dr),
respectively (Table 2, entries 27−28). However, in the case of
alkynes 1ac−1ae bearing secondary alkyl substituents (i-Pr,
cyclohexyl, cyclopentyl) at the alkyne terminus, a Sc(III)-
catalyzed tandem carbonyl−yne/cycloisomerization reaction
occurred, furnishing polycyclic 2,5-dihydrofuran products
2ac−2ae (Table 2, entries 29−30).
To elucidate the origin of diastereoselectivity in the
scandium-catalyzed formation of multisubstituted allenes,
density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed
(Figure 1).
24−38
The reaction initiates with coordination of the
α-ketoamide group to scandium trifluoromethanesulfonate,
forming intermediates INT1 and INT2. These intermediates
then undergo C−C bond formation and hydrogen migration,
giving INT3 and INT4 via transition states TS1 and TS2,
respectively. Subsequent decomplexation yields allenes 2a and
2a′. The calculated Gibbs free energy of activation (ΔG
‡
) for
the pathway via TS1 (8.7 kcal/mol) is 1.8 kcal/mol lower than
that for the TS2 pathway (10.5 kcal/mol), which is in excellent
agreement with the experimentally observed product distribu-
tion. Geometric analysis of TS1 indicates a concerted yet
asynchronous mechanism.
This asynchronicity is evidenced by the bond lengths within
the transition state structure: the forming C1−C2 bond (1.98
Å) is substantially formed, whereas the scissile C3−H bond is
marginally elongated to 1.12 from 1.09 Å, and the H−O bond
is only 2.16 Å. This disparity demonstrates that C−C bond
formation is significantly more advanced than C−H bond
cleavage.
A notable finding is that the overall free energy trend is
inverted relative to the electronic energies. TS2 is electroni-
cally more stable than TS1 by approximately 0.19 kcal/mol.
However, the diastereoselectivity is governed by the Gibbs free
energy, and the preference for the TS1 pathway is determined

TS1 possesses greater conformational and vibrational freedom,
which manifests as a larger population of low-frequency
vibrational modes. These modes make a substantial contribu-
tion to the vibrational entropy, thereby lowering the overall
Gibbs free energy of TS1. In contrast, in TS2, the motion of
the butyl group is sterically restricted by interactions with the
triflate anion. This restriction results in an increase in its
vibrational wavenumbers by approximately 5−10 cm

relative
to TS1, leading to a significant entropic penalty and rendering
this pathway less favorable. Furthermore, the influence of the
R
1

also be linked to dispersion forces. Interactions between R
1
and the n-butyl on the alkyne group could potentially narrow
the electronic energy difference between TS1 and TS2, thereby
affecting the reaction’s diastereoselectivity.
To demonstrate the synthetic potential of the Sc-catalyzed
carbonyl−yne reaction, we performed a series of trans-
formations on allene 2a (Figure 2). Treatment of 2a with
silver(I) triflate induced cyclization, affording dihydrofuran 3
in 76% yield. Alternatively, palladium-catalyzed cyclization/
allylation of 2a produced dihydrofuran 4. Employing N-
iodosuccinimide (NIS) provided dihydrofuran 5 in 70% yield.
Notably, the formation of dihydrofurans 3−5 proceeded
diastereoselectively, as confirmed by X-ray crystallographic
analysis. Under the promotion of N-bromosuccinimide (NBS),
2a underwent a semipinacol rearrangement featuring 1,2-
migration of the isopropyl group. This transformation
furnished trisubstituted alkene 6 as the major product, whose
structure was unambiguously confirmed by X-ray crystallo-
graphic analysis.
In summary, we have developed a Sc(OTf)
3
-catalyzed
carbonyl−yne reaction for the diastereoselective synthesis of
multisubstituted allenes from α-ketoamide-tethered alkynes.
This method features excellent atom economy, a broad
substrate scope (tolerating diverse alkyl, aryl, and functional
groups), and good-to-excellent diastereoselectivity. Theoretical
analysis suggests that the observed stereoselectivity arises from
a sophisticated interplay of electronic and entropic effects in
the transition states. Meanwhile, this work addresses long-
standing challenges in carbonyl−yne chemistry, establishing a
robust platform for allene synthesis with applications in target-
oriented synthesis. Further investigations into the asymmetric

To elucidate the origin of diastereoselectivity in the
scandium-catalyzed formation of multisubstituted allenes,
density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed
(Figure 1).<sup>24−38</sup> The reaction initiates with coordination of the
α-ketoamide group to scandium trifluoromethanesulfonate,
forming intermediates INT1 and INT2. These intermediates
then undergo C−C bond formation and hydrogen migration,
giving INT3 and INT4 via transition states TS1 and TS2,
respectively. Subsequent decomplexation yields allenes 2a and
2a′. The calculated Gibbs free energy of activation (ΔG<sup>‡</sup>) for
the pathway via TS1 (8.7 kcal/mol) is 1.8 kcal/mol lower than
that for the TS2 pathway (10.5 kcal/mol), which is in excellent
agreement with the experimentally observed product distribu-
tion. Geometric analysis of TS1 indicates a concerted yet
asynchronous mechanism.

This asynchronicity is evidenced by the bond lengths within
the transition state structure: the forming C1−C2 bond (1.98
Å) is substantially formed, whereas the scissile C3−H bond is
marginally elongated to 1.12 from 1.09 Å, and the H−O bond
is only 2.16 Å. This disparity demonstrates that C−C bond
formation is significantly more advanced than C−H bond
cleavage.

A notable finding is that the overall free energy trend is
inverted relative to the electronic energies. TS2 is electroni-
cally more stable than TS1 by approximately 0.19 kcal/mol.

To demonstrate the synthetic potential of the Sc-catalyzed

formations on allene 2a (Figure 2). Treatment of 2a with

structure was unambiguously confirmed by X-ray crystallo-

In summary, we have developed a Sc(OTf) -catalyzed
carbonyl−yne reaction for the diastereoselective synthesis of
multisubstituted allenes from α-ketoamide-tethered alkynes.
This method features excellent atom economy, a broad
substrate scope (tolerating diverse alkyl, aryl, and functional
groups), and good-to-excellent diastereoselectivity. Theoretical
analysis suggests that the observed stereoselectivity arises from
a sophisticated interplay of electronic and entropic efects in
the transition states. Meanwhile, this work addresses long-
standing challenges in carbonyl−yne chemistry, establishing a
robust platform for allene synthesis with applications in target-
